builder_plan.scenario: Your self-hosted model spends too long generating answers token by token.
builder_plan.change: Check whether a compatible draft model and serving integration exist before renting compute.
builder_plan.baseline: The same target with speculation off, then your existing drafter if you have one.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Accepted draft length, tokens per second, tail latency, output quality, and total GPU cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: APEX: Speculate smarter, not deeper
summary: It replaces fixed speculative decoding configurations (a single drafting method and a constant draft depth) with a request-level router among EAGLE-3, n-gram, and draft-model speculation plus block-level depth adaptation driven by verifier feedback. It costs training and maintenance of a learned survival-model controller, integration changes in the serving stack (vLLM), and the presence of multiple draft mechanisms resident in memory, though the target model and its verification procedure are unchanged. It can fail when controller signals mispredict acceptance on out-of-distribution workloads, when EAGLE-3 or draft-model heads are unavailable for the deployed model, or when the speedup does not transfer from the reported Qwen3-8B setup to other models or traffic mixes.
rationale: Speculative decoding is directly deployable on a single 24 GB GPU via vLLM and the claimed latency gains are large, but the controller is validated only on one model and six workloads, so the reader should validate it on their own traffic before production adoption.
technique: Adaptive controller for speculative decoding depth and expert selection

claims.statement: It replaces fixed speculative decoding configurations (a single drafting method and a constant draft depth) with a request-level router among EAGLE-3, n-gram, and draft-model speculation plus block-level depth adaptation driven by verifier feedback. It costs training and maintenance of a learned survival-model controller, integration changes in the serving stack (vLLM), and the presence of multiple draft mechanisms resident in memory, though the target model and its verification procedure are unchanged. It can fail when controller signals mispredict acceptance on out-of-distribution workloads, when EAGLE-3 or draft-model heads are unavailable for the deployed model, or when the speedup does not transfer from the reported Qwen3-8B setup to other models or traffic mixes.

APEX-S achieves 4.27x aggregate speedup over autoregressive decoding (up to 5.24x per workload) with Qwen3-8B in vLLM; APEX-B gives 3.27x with 41.0% relative reduction in wasted-token percentage vs fixed n-gram speculation at k=16.
